clue.text: A charge on making port in Alaska

indicators.note: making signals that the letters of the preceding words are worked up into something new, an anagram

explanation.surface: Someone pays a fee on arriving at a harbour in Alaska.
explanation.walkthrough: 'making' is the anagram signal: the letters of A CHARGE ON are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Anchorage is the largest city of Alaska and a harbour on Cook Inlet.

clue.text: Poet appearing to agree to disagree at first

indicators.note: at first places the disagreeing word ahead of the agreeing one in the answer

parts.note: to disagree is to say no
to agree is to say yes

explanation.surface: A poet seems willing to agree to disagree.
explanation.walkthrough: Alfred Noyes was an English poet, author of 'The Highwayman'. 'at first' sets the disagreeing word ahead in the answer, though the clue names agreeing first.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred Noyes was an English writer of verse, best known for 'The Highwayman'.

clue.text: One over the eight, in a measure

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means the first piece sits above the second

parts.note: H is hydrogen, element number one
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone slightly drunk ('one over the eight') in a measure of drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One over the eight' is a British idiom for being a little drunk, but here hydrogen (H), element one, is put over EIGHT in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Height is a dimension that can be measured, how tall something stands.

clue.text: Bart's founder, a man in uncommon habit

indicators.note: in places the man inside the word for uncommon

parts.note: uncommon means rare
he is a man, the male pronoun

explanation.surface: The founder of St Bartholomew's was a man in an unusual monk's habit.
explanation.walkthrough: Bart's is St Bartholomew's Hospital in London, founded in 1123 by the monk Rahere; 'habit' adds to the picture and gives no letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Rahere, a courtier turned Augustinian canon, established St Bartholomew's Priory and Hospital in London.

clue.text: Shades of a Dickensian Sarah?

parts.note: Sarah Gamp, the nurse in Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit, always carried an umbrella, so umbrellas (shades) came to be named after her

explanation.surface: Ghosts of a woman from a Dickens novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shades' suggests ghosts; here it means sunshades, umbrellas. In British slang an umbrella is a gamp, after Mrs Sarah Gamp in Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit.
explanation.definitionFit: Umbrellas are called this in old British slang, after the brolly-carrying nurse in Martin Chuzzlewit.

clue.text: Possible diagnosis of shooting-pains

parts.note: shooting pains read as pains from being shot, so the cause would be metal bullets in the body

explanation.surface: A doctor names the cause of a patient's sharp stabbing pains.
explanation.walkthrough: Shooting pains are sharp stabbing pains, but read literally they come from being shot, and bullets are made of lead.
explanation.definitionFit: Toxic illness from a heavy metal, here imagined as the result of being hit by bullets.

clue.text: Honest blonde not caring for modern rhythm?

definitions.meaning: honest dealing is straightforward and just

definitions.text: blonde not caring for modern rhythm
definitions.meaning: fair means blonde, and someone square has no time for modern music, so a blonde and a square together

explanation.surface: A truthful fair-haired person with no taste for new music.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the phrase: FAIR (blonde) AND SQUARE (old-fashioned, not into modern rhythm), with the question mark flagging the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: Above board and just: the idiom for dealing straightforwardly; also a fair-haired person and an unhip one.

clue.text: Food taken after a flare up at sea?

definitions.text: Food taken after a flare up at sea?

parts.words: Food taken after a flare up at sea?
parts.note: a Very light is a signal flare fired from a pistol, so a meal eaten after one goes up at sea

explanation.surface: Something to eat after a quarrel flares up on board ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flare up' suggests a row; it is a Very light, a coloured flare fired as a distress signal, followed by a meal. Read normally, the phrase means something tiny to eat.
explanation.definitionFit: A small snack, made of a signal flare (Very light) followed by food.

clue.text: Run off with theologian in wild Sarah

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Run off with theologian in wild Sarah': DD (theologian) leaves SKEALE+D to come from 'wild Sarah', which has no such letters; 'Sarah' looks carried over from 5-down and the true fodder is missing
annotationWithheld.clue: Run off with theologian in wild Sarah

clue.text: There to see the finish of a Tourist Trophy race?

indicators.note: of puts the finish after the race it belongs to

parts.note: the TT is the Isle of Man Tourist Trophy motorcycle race
a finish is an ending

explanation.surface: Being present to watch the end of an Isle of Man motorbike race.
explanation.walkthrough: The TT is the Tourist Trophy motorcycle race on the Isle of Man. 'the finish of a TT race' reads as A TT ENDING.
explanation.definitionFit: Being present at an event, there to see it, is attending it.

clue.text: Credit we get from the Greeks

definitions.text: Credit we get from the Greeks

parts.words: Credit we get from the Greeks
parts.note: the word for praise or prestige was borrowed into English from Greek

explanation.surface: Praise we owe to ancient Greece.
explanation.definitionFit: Prestige or praise; English took the word from Greek, where it means glory.

clue.text: Mackerel bait

parts.note: the saying 'a ... to catch a mackerel' means a small outlay to win a big prize

explanation.surface: Something to put on the hook for mackerel.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'throw a sprat to catch a mackerel' means risking a little to gain a lot.
explanation.definitionFit: A small fish of the herring family, the proverb's small lure for a bigger catch.

clue.text: The English girl in the Spanish dress

indicators.note: to dress is to arrange or set in order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the word 'the' in English
el is Spanish for the

explanation.surface: An English girl wearing a Spanish dress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dress' looks like a garment; it is the anagram signal, rearranging THE plus EL (Spanish 'the').
explanation.definitionFit: A female given name, so an example of a girl.

clue.text: Gave ear to the Cockney and miscalculated

indicators.note: the Cockney drops the h, so the word is said the East London way

parts.note: to give ear to something is to have heard it

explanation.surface: Someone listened to a Londoner and got the sums wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockneys (working-class East Londoners) drop their h's: 'heard' becomes 'eard, said like ERRED.
explanation.definitionFit: To have miscalculated is to have made a mistake, to have gone wrong.

clue.text: Composer, one of a number in a crowd

indicators.note: in places the number inside the crowd

parts.note: a host is a great crowd
L is the Roman numeral fifty

explanation.surface: A composer is just one person among many in a crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one of a number' points to L, one Roman numeral (fifty), put inside HOST.
explanation.definitionFit: Gustav Holst was an English composer, best known for The Planets.

clue.text: Substitute in practice

parts.note: a stand-in doctor working in a medical practice while the regular one is away

explanation.surface: In reality, a replacement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in practice' looks like 'in reality'; it means a doctor's practice.
explanation.definitionFit: A temporary stand-in doctor or cleric covering for an absent one.

clue.text: Evergreen tree strangely adored

indicators.note: strangely says the letters of the next word are in an odd order

explanation.surface: An evergreen that is oddly loved.
explanation.definitionFit: A Himalayan cedar, a conifer that keeps its needles all year.

clue.text: Studies Old English around Hans Andersen's birthplace

indicators.note: around puts the old English letters on either side of the studies

parts.note: dens are private studies

explanation.surface: Researching Old English in the Danish town where the storyteller was born.
explanation.definitionFit: The Danish city on Funen where the fairytale author Hans Christian Andersen was born in 1805.

clue.text: Souvenir of high priest preserved by Christian denomination

indicators.note: preserved by means held inside the denomination

parts.note: RC is Roman Catholic
Eli was the high priest who raised Samuel in the Bible

explanation.surface: A keepsake of a high priest kept by a church.
explanation.walkthrough: Eli is the Old Testament high priest who brought up Samuel.
explanation.definitionFit: A keepsake or memento kept from the past.

clue.text: Issued order to abandon practice

indicators.note: order means the letters are put into a new sequence

explanation.surface: An order is issued to give up a custom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'order' looks like a command; it is the anagram signal for ISSUED.
explanation.definitionFit: To stop using something, give up a custom; the verb sense of no longer using.

clue.text: Not accustomed to what is new

explanation.surface: Someone unfamiliar with novelty.
explanation.definitionFit: Not familiar with (unused to) and also untouched, never put to use.

clue.text: In fact, a singular bit of information

definitions.text: In fact, a singular bit of information

parts.words: In fact, a singular bit of information
parts.note: a single fact; the plural, data, is the more familiar form

explanation.surface: Really, one remarkable piece of news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'singular' looks like 'remarkable'; it is the grammatical singular of data.
explanation.definitionFit: A single piece of information; data is its plural.

clue.text: Equally an expansive person

definitions.meaning: ... is a grand, showy person, and to swell is to expand

explanation.surface: Likewise, someone generous.
explanation.definitionFit: Meaning too or also, and read as a swell, a grandly dressed showy gent.

clue.text: More imaginative country

parts.note: Thomas More's imagined ideal island state in his 1516 book

explanation.surface: A nation with greater creativity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'More' looks like a comparative; it is Sir Thomas More, whose 1516 book named an imagined ideal land.
explanation.definitionFit: An ideal society; Thomas More's book gave the name to any perfect imagined place.

clue.text: Fish round for a native tongue

parts.note: ling is a fish of the cod family
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: Fishing around for the local language.
explanation.definitionFit: A colloquial word for a language or jargon.

clue.text: Notable work over a period

indicators.note: in a down clue, over puts the work above the period

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work
an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: An important piece produced over some time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notable' read as 'full of notes' defines a staged musical work.
explanation.definitionFit: A dramatic work full of notes sung, so something note-able.

clue.text: Bear a different name

parts.note: an old nickname for a bear, from the bear in the Reynard the Fox tales

explanation.surface: Go by another name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bear' looks like a verb (to carry a name); it is the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The traditional storybook name for a bear, from the Reynard the Fox tales.

clue.text: Ruins pieces of sculpture

definitions.meaning: to bust something is to break or ruin it
sculptures of a head and shoulders

explanation.surface: Wrecks statues.
explanation.definitionFit: Breaks (wrecks) and also head-and-shoulders sculptures.

clue.text: Process likely to produce only a faint likeness

definitions.text: Process likely to produce only a faint likeness

parts.words: Process likely to produce only a faint likeness
parts.note: a photograph given too little light comes out pale and faint

explanation.surface: A method that gives a weak resemblance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Process' is photographic processing: too little light on the film gives a pale picture.
explanation.definitionFit: In photography, giving film too little light, so the image is pale.

clue.text: Just the thing if you want to hit the hay

definitions.text: Just the thing if you want to hit the hay

parts.words: Just the thing if you want to hit the hay
parts.note: to hit the hay is to go to bed, and this mattress is stuffed with straw

explanation.surface: Ideal when you are ready to go to bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hit the hay' means go to bed; the bed in question is literally stuffed with straw.
explanation.definitionFit: A straw-filled mattress, a simple bed.
